changelog.the_reversal: Ruling 1 said the API was a REPLICA and the client's local commit was the write path. Reversed: 'some should be on the phone for speed, but there should not be a replica on the phone.' The server owns the data; the phone keeps a disposable cache so screens open instantly; with no signal, reads work from the cache and writes are BLOCKED with a reason. No queue, no outbox, no deferred writes. Delete the cache and nothing is lost.
what_the_v3_brief_got_wrong_about_the_cl: THE BRIEF SAID: '`logbookProvider` becomes async, and screens that have no loading states grow them.' THAT IS WRONG AND IT WOULD HAVE BEEN THE MOST EXPENSIVE MISTAKE IN THE PLAN — it implied rewriting roughly thirty providers and eighteen screens. MEASURED: `main.dart` already awaits `openLogbook()` BEFORE `runApp` and hands the result to `logbookSeedProvider` through `startupOverrides`, and its own comment says why, verbatim at main.dart:20 — 'There is no loading state because there is no frame in which the log is unknown.' A cache file is read by exactly the same mechanism as a log file. `logbookProvider` stays SYNCHRONOUS, no `AsyncValue` is pushed anywhere, and no screen grows a spinner. What is added is a background refresh AFTER the first frame. This is the difference between a client change measured in days and one measured in weeks, and it is corrected in docs/CLIENT-PREREQUISITES.md rather than surviving as an instruction.

THE BRIEF SAID: design 'read shapes that match screens' and be honest about round trips. Overtaken by the same measurement. The log is 85,422 bytes and the phone holds all of it, so screens derive locally exactly as they do today and there are no per-screen reads to design. Cache validation is for ONE whole-log refresh. Any per-screen endpoint would be a second way to get data the phone already has — see DEC-31.
withdrawn: DEC-03 — the device-id / per-device-sequence tension. There is no device identity problem when there is one authoritative copy. `X-Device-Id`, `X-Op-Seq` and `409 op_out_of_order` are gone.

DEC-04 — the last-write-wins conflict rule, AND WITH IT AN ACCEPTED SILENT DATA LOSS. This is the best thing v3 buys back and it is worth stating plainly. v2 ruled that a delete always beats a concurrent update, so a rename made on one device could be silently destroyed by a delete made on another, with nothing to report it — a data-loss rule stated on purpose and flagged for the human to overrule. It is not softened or deferred: with one authoritative copy the failure it managed CANNOT OCCUR. Two phones editing one trip is now ordinary last-request-wins against a live server, which is what a system of record does and is not silent loss.

decisions.status: kept in its FK half; TOMBSTONE HALF WITHDRAWN
decisions.title: Hard deletes with FK cascades. The tombstones and their AFTER DELETE triggers are gone
decisions.evidence: The critic verified the mapping row by row and reported it correct. D3: photos/walks/visits cascade on trip_id, PLACES SURVIVE, and a surviving photo naming a dead visit gets visit_id SET NULL — which IS `_repointed`. D2: visits cascade from the place; photos either go or lose place_id AND visit_id together — which IS `Photo.copyWith(clearPlace:true)`; walks untouched because Walk has no place_id to cascade from.
decisions.reasoning: The cascades are untouched and must not be disturbed — the schema IS the delete sheets' copy, which is the strongest form of the client's own doctrine. What goes is the tombstone side: a cache is never TOLD what was deleted, it re-fetches. Six triggers, one table and a `kind='visit'` reporting problem the client's codec could never have consumed all disappear with the requirement that produced them.
decisions.consequence: Six FKs and one deliberate absence, each carrying a comment quoting the sheet line it implements. GUARDS UNCHANGED: a wishlist place survives its trip's deletion, and a place whose ONLY visits were on the deleted trip also survives with zero visits. The critic's observation stands that the server's SET NULL is slightly MORE correct than the client here, because it also catches another place's photograph naming one of the deleted visits.

decisions.status: kept, with the writer justification restated and the reader half now more important
decisions.title: Writes take a per-traveller advisory lock; reads take a repeatable-read snapshot
decisions.evidence: The critic set out to break the writer argument and reported it sound. The client made the same call for itself: 'Two writeAsString calls racing on one path can interleave, and an interleaved log is a corrupt one.'
decisions.reasoning: RESTATED FOR v3, because half its old justification is gone. The lock is no longer about a gap-free replication cursor — there is no cursor. What remains is real and enough: `PUT /v1/places/{id}` replaces a whole ordered visits array (delete then reinsert), `POST /refile` is a read-modify-write, `PUT /v1/cities/{id}?attachTo` touches two tables, and DEC-02's cross-kind EXISTS check is only race-free under it. THE READER HALF GOT MORE IMPORTANT, not less: reads are now the PRIMARY path, and a torn read across the six lists would be served to a phone that caches it and stops asking.
decisions.consequence: `store.WithTravellerTx` (advisory lock) is the only place a traveller-scoped WRITE transaction opens. `store.WithReadSnapshot` opens `BeginTx` at `sql.LevelRepeatableRead` and the ETag is computed INSIDE that snapshot — otherwise the phone can cache a body under a version number that does not describe it, which is the one cache bug that never self-corrects. A read-only repeatable-read transaction in Postgres never hits a serialization failure, so this costs a held snapshot and nothing else.

decisions.status: WITHDRAWN in v3, superseded by DEC-33
decisions.title: [WITHDRAWN] Idempotency-Key on every mutating request, committed inside the transaction
decisions.evidence: Its strongest surviving justification in v2 was that a retried PUT racing a TOMBSTONE answers 409 where the original answered 200, stalling a serial worker. Tombstones are gone and so is the worker.
decisions.reasoning: See DEC-33: every verb is already idempotent because the client mints every id, and the one thing that broke that went with the replication model.
decisions.consequence: The middleware, the `operations` table, the `request_fingerprint`, the 64 KiB response cap and the codes `idempotency_mismatch` and `replay_unavailable` are all gone. SF3's transaction-boundary bug — the operations row landing after the handler's tx committed — is not fixed, it is deleted.

decisions.status: kept, RULED
decisions.title: Passphrase KDF is Argon2id via golang.org/x/crypto/argon2
decisions.evidence: go_backend.md L24 specifies the SESSION TOKEN hash and says nothing about the passphrase. sha256 of a passphrase is unsalted and GPU-trivial. MEASURED: x/crypto forces the go directive to `go 1.25.0`; `go 1.22` AND `go 1.25` both fail build and vet.
decisions.reasoning: The only memory-hard choice, Go-team maintained. Alternatives were stdlib pbkdf2 (raises the floor anyway, so buys nothing), pinning x/crypto v0.31.0 (freezes the one dependency that matters at December 2024), and hand-rolled PBKDF2 (stdlib-pure, not memory-hard).
decisions.consequence: argon2.IDKey behind `internal/auth.Hasher` — one interface, one implementation, so a swap is one file. Per-user 16-byte crypto/rand salt, encoded `$argon2id$v=19$m=..,t=..,p=..$salt$hash` so parameters travel with the hash. Two external modules, not one: x/sys arrives transitively via blake2b. PARAMETERS UNTUNED — 64 MiB / t=1 / p=4 is the OWASP starting point, it is a memory ceiling per concurrent login, it competes with DB_MAX_OPEN_CONNS for the same RAM, and DEC-36's direct-to-bucket upload exists partly so multi-megabyte transfers never join that contest.

decisions.status: kept
decisions.title: NAMED DIVERGENCE 1 (from the SPEC): the Dockerfile build stage is golang:1.26, not golang:1.22
decisions.evidence: Ruling 4: 'Build on Go 1.26 ... Record this as a deliberate, named divergence from the spec — do not bury it.'
decisions.reasoning: A 1.22 build image and a 1.26 development toolchain produce binaries from different compilers, runtimes and std sources. The spec's INTENT — a reproducible multi-stage build into scratch — is fully honoured; only the tag moves. And with the module floor at 1.25.0, a golang:1.22 stage could not compile this module at all.

decisions.status: kept, RULED (plaintext)
decisions.title: The share link is a capability the CLIENT mints; the server stores it in plaintext so `Trip.shareLinkId` round-trips
decisions.evidence: `shareLinkId` is on the client's Trip codec and is the whole basis of H1: `travellog.app/l/${trip.shareLinkId}`, and 'Stop sharing' only appears when it is non-null. Storing only a hash means the server cannot emit it, so a phone with a cold cache shows a trip as NOT SHARED while a live public link to it exists.
decisions.reasoning: The trade is owned rather than waved away: the same database dump already contains every note, caption, coordinate and photograph row those links expose, so the marginal loss is the ability to keep reading AFTER the dump — which revocation covers.
decisions.consequence: `share_links(traveller_id, trip_id, token text UNIQUE, created_at, revoked_at)`. 'Never existed' and 'revoked' are the SAME 404 with the same work done, so nothing confirms a guessed token was once real. The constant-time compare defends the REVOCATION ORACLE, not guessing — guessing is defended by the 31^12 keyspace and the rate limiter, and an indexed equality lookup is not constant-time and cannot be made so. THE LOG PROBLEM, which neither v1 nor the critique caught: the token is in the URL path, so `/l/{token}` writes a live capability into slog's access log and Caddy's. A path redactor rewrites anything under `/l/` to `/l/[redacted]`, the Caddyfile omits the request URI for that route, and a leg asserts the token bytes are absent from the logger's output.

decisions.status: AMENDED IN PLACE at v5 (V4-SF1) — twelve codes, and the count is re-derived from the const block
decisions.title: Error bodies are `{"code":"…"}` with a closed vocabulary and no prose, ever
decisions.evidence: The client's design system has no toast and refuses one; every failure surface is a fixed per-surface sentence the CLIENT owns.
decisions.reasoning: Prose the server sends is prose the server must translate, style and keep consistent with a design system it cannot see. The vocabulary must be CLOSED or it drifts into prose by accretion.
decisions.consequence:
One const block in internal/httpx is the whole vocabulary, and at v5 it holds TWELVE: `unauthenticated`, `forbidden`, `not_found`, `conflict`, `invalid_body`, `invalid_field`, `rate_limited`, `payload_too_large`, `timeout`, `internal`, `upload_incomplete`, and `unsupported_format` (DEC-53). v4 said 'SHRUNK FROM FOURTEEN TO ELEVEN' and listed eleven while DEC-53 added a twelfth — AND THAT WAS MECHANICAL, NOT COSMETIC: the guard below asserts every literal passed to WriteError is IN the const block, so a block built from the stated eleven reddens the sweep the moment S13 writes the twelfth. THE COUNT IS RE-DERIVED FROM THE BLOCK, never remembered — `grep -c '^\s*Code' internal/httpx/errors.go` — the same discipline `base.measured` applies to the route table.

GONE with their rulings: `deleted`, `op_out_of_order`, `idempotency_mismatch`, `replay_unavailable`.

An AST walk collects every literal passed to WriteError and asserts each is in the const block — MECHANISM, not discipline. `timeout` is load-bearing: `http.TimeoutHandler` writes ITS OWN body, so the handler is constructed with a message that IS the JSON envelope — the one response the sweep structurally cannot see is the one stdlib writes. One optional additive key is allowed: `field` on invalid_field. Real detail goes to slog with the request id, never to the body.

decisions.status: kept; interacts with DEC-40
decisions.title: Two version numbers, two meanings; every server addition is additive-and-optional
decisions.evidence: `logbookFormatVersion = 1`; `decodeLogbook` throws a FormatException on any other value and `LogbookStore.load` turns that into the quarantine path.
decisions.reasoning: `/v1` in the path is the API contract version; `"version": N` in the body is the LOGBOOK FORMAT version and belongs to the client's codecs. Conflating them means an API refactor breaks every phone.
decisions.consequence: Golden key-list files per response shape; a diff is a review event. The version is emitted by exactly one function taking it as a parameter. DEC-40 moves that parameter's value to 2 and explains why that is cheap NOW and expensive LATER — the rule changes the moment the client ships against this server.

decisions.status: kept
decisions.title: Preferences are not stored server-side
decisions.evidence: The client's own decision: preferences.json is a second file with its own store and defaults; 'how precisely THIS phone takes a reading is not part of anybody's record'.
decisions.reasoning: `ImportRule` and `LocationAccuracy` are properties of a handset, not of a log. Under v3 this gets STRONGER, not weaker: the log is now server-owned, and a handset setting is the clearest possible example of something that is not.

decisions.status: kept, AMENDED by DEC-41
decisions.title: There are still no real photographs, and that fact survives the move to object storage
decisions.evidence: Every `Photo.asset` is one of two bundled sample PNGs. `Photo.image` is a getter and appears in no `_$...ToJson` — the wire carries `asset` only, confirmed by the critic against photo.g.dart. The shutter is inert by decision: 'The camera shutter would persist a fiction... there is no capture behind it... Recommendation: do not wire it.' The client's export decision makes the same point: copying the assets out 'would hand somebody sample imagery under a claim it is their holiday'.
decisions.reasoning: v2 responded to this by excluding photograph bytes entirely — no upload, no serving, and `asset` emitted at no setting in the public envelope. The human has now ruled that v1 BUILDS and SEEDS the media path, so the exclusion is lifted. THE UNDERLYING FACT IS NOT LIFTED WITH IT, and keeping the two apart is the whole point of amending this decision rather than deleting it: building a pipeline is not the same as having something true to put through it.
decisions.consequence: AMENDED: the media path exists (DEC-36, DEC-37, DEC-38) and is seeded through its own real routes (DEC-41). WHAT DOES NOT CHANGE: what flows through it is stock imagery, and no traveller's log gains a photograph they did not take — a real registration yields an EMPTY log, because DEC-18's adopt is withdrawn and nothing imports the fixture. So the seeded objects are reachable only by a fixture that references them. THE README SAYS THIS PLAINLY rather than leaving a share link to imply otherwise. TRIGGER for `asset` meaning a real photograph: a real capture in the client, which is the dependency conversation the client's own record has been holding open.

decisions.status: kept, extended
decisions.title: Two test seams, and which is which is stated rather than blended
decisions.evidence: The behaviours worth guarding ARE the SQL: SET NULL on photos.visit_id is `_repointed`; the cascade from places to visits is D2's 'the visits go with the pin'; the ABSENCE of a cascade to places is D3's 'the pins stay in those cities'.
decisions.reasoning: An interface seam over the store lets every one of those legs pass against a fake that implements the cascade in Go — proving the fake, not the schema. But making the whole suite need Docker makes a green `go test ./...` without Docker a lie.
decisions.consequence: internal/store tests call `testdb.Open(t)`, which skips with a message naming `make test-db` — and the message is itself asserted. Handler tests run against the `logbook.Store` interface in memory, table-driven, asserting response BYTES. EXTENDED IN v3: object storage gets the same treatment — `objects.Store` is an interface, handler tests use an in-memory implementation, and the SigV4 presigner is tested against MinIO in the same gated way (`TEST_S3_ENDPOINT`), because a presigner that is wrong 403s against real S3 and passes against a fake.

decisions.status: kept
decisions.title: A hand-rolled migration runner over embed.FS, not goose or golang-migrate
decisions.evidence: The spec forbids third-party routers, ORMs, JSON and validation libraries; a migration tool is the same class.
decisions.reasoning: The whole runner is ~60 lines with visible failure modes. A tool brings a CLI, a config format, a lock protocol and a version-drift story for something a deploy runs once. Down files are checked in — they are the only real review of an up migration — and never run automatically.
decisions.consequence: //go:embed, one transaction per file, a database-wide advisory lock so two replicas cannot race on boot, and a LOUD checksum failure on a file edited after it was applied. v3 needs ONE migration where v2 needed two, because the entire sync-table migration went with the replication model.

decisions.status: kept, RULED
decisions.title: The repo grows its own CLAUDE.md, written step by step as the work lands
decisions.evidence: The Flutter CLAUDE.md carries measurements, declined alternatives and constraints the code cannot express — and notes four counts that went wrong from reconstruction after the fact.
decisions.reasoning: A record written while the reasoning is fresh is trustworthy; one reconstructed at the end is how stale counts and wrong justifications get in.
decisions.consequence: Every step appends what it decided, measured or declined to CLAUDE.md in the SAME COMMIT as its code. It must carry: the spec constraints and how each is honoured; the gate and why vet is mandatory; the two test seams; the client-facing invariants (the permissive id rule, the unknown-id asymmetry, the cascade table, and the three-way token boundary — SESSION tokens hashed, SHARE tokens plaintext, MEDIA URLs signed and expiring); and a re-derivable route count with its command. STANDING INSTRUCTION: when a claim is corrected, record WHAT WAS WRONG and how it was measured, not only the corrected fact — v3 corrects two of the brief's own instructions and both corrections are worth more than the facts that replaced them.

decisions.status: AMENDED IN PLACE at v5 (V4-B2) — the key rule was never a row rule, and `places` is the derived collection
decisions.title: The public envelope is an explicit ALLOWLIST, defined before a line of the public read is written
decisions.evidence: v1's central privacy guard was unsatisfiable: it demanded `"lat"` be absent while deliberately keeping `cities.centre`, which serialises as `{"lat":..,"lng":..}`. It was also VACUOUS — `Photo` has no flat `lat` key, so a test against `"lat"` would have passed against a leak of the whole `coordinates` object.
decisions.reasoning: A denylist exposes every future field by default and can only test the fields somebody remembered — which is exactly how v1 missed `Place.plan`, `Trip.summary` and `Walk.name`. An allowlist inverts it: anything not enumerated is absent by construction. CLASSIFYING RULE: is this field THE THING BEING SHARED, or an ANNOTATION ON IT? `Trip.name` is obviously kept, so 'the traveller wrote it' cannot be the criterion.
decisions.consequence:
docs/PUBLIC-ENVELOPE.md is written and reviewed BEFORE the public read is built. ALWAYS: trip {id,name,start,end,summary}; cities [{id,name,country,centre}]; places [{id,cityId,name}]; walks [{id,cityId,recordedOn,distanceKm,name}]. IF sharePhotos: photos [{id,cityId,placeId,takenAt}] — AND, NEW IN v3, `media:{url,expiresAt}` per photo, a presigned read URL minted server-side (DEC-37). IF shareNotes: `note`, `caption`, `plan`. IF shareCoordinates: `coordinates` on places and photos, `accuracyMetres`, `points` on walks. NEVER: `asset` (the raw object id — the browser gets a URL or nothing), `coverAsset`, `filedLater`, `dismissed`, `visitId`, `tripId`, `shareLinkId`, the three flags, the traveller.

WITH `sharePhotos: false` NO URL IS MINTED AT ALL — not an unusable one, not an expired one, not a 403. The photos key is absent and no presign call is made. THE GUARD IS STRUCTURAL: parse the response, walk it, assert the emitted key set at every level EQUALS the allowlist. That is what lets the city centre stay visible — the assertion becomes 'the only `lat` in this document is under `cities[].centre`'. Eight golden files, one per flag combination.

AND THE META-CHECK SURVIVES VERBATIM, because it is the best line in the plan: select a coordinate column and zero it in Go instead — the structural leg must STILL redden, because the key would still be emitted. If it does not redden, the test is worthless and must be rewritten.

*** THE ROW RULE, WHICH v4 NEVER STATED AND WHICH THE KEY-SET GUARD IS BLIND TO BY CONSTRUCTION. *** 'Anything not enumerated is absent' governs KEYS. It cannot tell four places from four hundred. And `places` is the one collection here that is NOT stored against the trip: places belong to the CITY and accumulate across trips, so a trip's places are DERIVED. Emit places for the trip's cities and the share page leaks every other trip's pins in those cities AND every wishlist place the traveller never visited — on the one step this plan calls 'a leak rather than a bug'.
ROWS, stated beside the keys:
- `places`: those with AT LEAST ONE VISIT whose `trip_id` is this trip. The client's own derivation is `all.where((p) => p.visitedOn(tripId))` (logbook.dart:1073) over `visitsOn(tripId).isNotEmpty` (place.dart:112).
- `photos` and `walks`: filter on their own `trip_id` column. Safe by construction.
- `cities`: from `trips.city_ids`. Safe by construction.
- `visits` inside a place: only those with this `trip_id`, or the notes of other trips leak through a place that is legitimately present.
THE LEG THE KEY-SET WALK CANNOT SUBSTITUTE FOR: a fixture holding a wishlist place AND a second trip's place in the same city, asserting NEITHER appears. MUTATION PROOF: drop the visit join from the places projection — THE KEY-SET LEG STAYS GREEN, and EVIDENCE.md records that this leg is the only thing that reddens. That is the clearest example in the plan of a guard that looks total and is not.

decisions.status: WITHDRAWN in v3, replaced by DEC-30
decisions.title: [WITHDRAWN] The replication change cursor and its six triggers
decisions.evidence: A per-row monotonic cursor so a second device could pull only what changed. There is no second copy to bring up to date.
decisions.reasoning: It was the most intricate thing in v2 and every part of it was forced by per-ROW reporting: a global sequence, BEFORE UPDATE triggers on six tables (because a DEFAULT is evaluated on INSERT and never again), an AFTER trigger on visits bumping the parent place (because Visit is nested inside Place in the client's codec and a `kind='visit'` tombstone is not something that codec can consume), and no-op suppression (because two devices re-PUTting what they pulled would otherwise bump each other's cursors forever).
decisions.consequence: ALL OF IT GOES, and with it the entire second migration. Cache validation needs to answer one question — 'has anything changed?' — not 'which rows changed since when?'. DEC-30 is one integer column and one line of Go. THE PING-PONG RISK DISAPPEARS WITH THE THING THAT CAUSED IT: there is no cursor to bump, so there is nothing to bump back.

decisions.status: AMENDED IN PLACE at v5 (V4-B5) — the ordinal rule for a visit CREATED by refile
decisions.title: Ordered child collections are jsonb or carry an explicit ordinal, and the integrity they lose moves into Go
decisions.evidence: `database/sql` has no array support through the pgx stdlib seam [assumed]. And v1's stated reason for rejecting a join table was simply WRONG — a join table with an ordinal preserves order exactly. Separately, `walks.points` appeared nowhere in v1's table list at all. And the client's refile reuses an occasion POSITIONALLY (`visitsOn(tripId).firstOrNull`), where SQL without ORDER BY has no defined first.
decisions.reasoning: Every column becomes a scalar or a jsonb blob, so no driver-specific type support is needed and spec L20 is honoured without hand-rolled literal escaping. jsonb also routes through `encoding/json`, which spec L19 already makes the only JSON package — one choice satisfying two constraints. Visits stay ROWS because DEC-05's cascades need them to be, so they get an ordinal instead.
decisions.consequence:
`trips.city_ids jsonb`, `walks.points jsonb`, `visits.ordinal int` with every read `ORDER BY ordinal`. The ordinal is load-bearing for the READ, not only for refile: emit visits in a different order and the client's `firstOrNull` flips, silently rebinding a photograph to a different occasion. THE INTEGRITY THIS COSTS, NAMED: jsonb `city_ids` cannot be FK-checked, so `PUT /v1/trips/{id}` must reject a body naming a city the traveller does not hold, in Go, with its own leg and its own mutation proof. Neither could `char(12)[]`, so it is not a regression — but a join table WOULD have had it, and choosing jsonb declines it knowingly.

THE ORDINAL A REFILE-CREATED VISIT GETS, which v4 left unstated on the one route DEC-26 was written for. Ordinals were supplied by the client only on `PUT /v1/places/{id}`, but `POST /v1/photos/{id}/refile` is the OTHER route that inserts a visit, and append-at-max is the obvious implementation and is WRONG: the client inserts the visit and re-sorts the place's whole list by `at` DESCENDING (`p.withVisits([...p.visits, visit]..sort((a,b) => b.at.compareTo(a.at)))`). Two readers depend on that order — `visitsOn(tripId).firstOrNull`, which refile itself reads, and `lastVisited => visits.first.at`. RULE: a visit created by refile takes the ordinal that keeps the place's visits in `at` DESC order, and THE WHOLE PLACE'S ORDINALS ARE REWRITTEN IN THAT TRANSACTION.
RULED AT v5, THE BODY SHAPE: `{placeId, visitId, visitAt}` — THE CLIENT MINTS BOTH. That keeps DEC-33's idempotency argument intact with no second server-minted id needing the treatment content addressing gave the first, and it is the smaller client change: one call site, M2.2. The client's `refilePhoto(photoId, placeId)` gains two arguments; CLIENT-PREREQUISITES carries it.

decisions.status: kept
decisions.title: NAMED DIVERGENCE 2 (from RULING 4, not the spec): the go.mod directive is `go 1.25.0`
decisions.evidence: MEASURED: x/crypto forces `go 1.25.0`. `go 1.22` fails both build and vet. AND `go 1.25` ALSO fails both — x/crypto v0.55.0 and x/sys v0.47.0 each declare `go 1.25.0`, and the directive comparison treats `1.25` as strictly lower. The literal string matters.
decisions.reasoning: Ruling 4's stated intent was that the shipped binary and the development toolchain match; raising the floor serves that intent rather than defying it. The human amended the ruling AFTER the measurement rather than in ignorance of it, and that ordering is the point.
decisions.consequence: go.mod's directive is written LITERALLY as `go 1.25.0` — an S01 acceptance check, not a note. FILED CORRECTLY: a divergence from ruling 4, NOT from the spec, because L17 says 'Go 1.22 or higher' and 1.25.0 satisfies it. Contrast DEC-39, which IS a spec divergence. Filing them the same way would put a false entry in the document a later reader trusts most.

decisions.status: kept
decisions.title: Every acceptance check must be able to fail for the right reason; three of v1's could not
decisions.evidence: MEASURED: `http.ServeMux` has no exported pattern enumeration in Go 1.26, so v1's 'walk the mux's registered patterns' was unimplementable and would have been silently downgraded to a grep. `grep BeginTx == 1 line` was false against correct code (the migration runner opens transactions by design) and blind to `db.Begin(`. `pg_dump --schema-only` compared byte-for-byte false-reds on a minor version bump and cannot see a schema dumped from itself.
decisions.reasoning: The client's own rule 10 turned on the plan's own checks. A check that cannot fail is worse than no check, because it is counted as coverage.
decisions.consequence: 1. ROUTES registered from a declared `[]Route{{Method,Pattern,Handler,Auth,Mutating}}` slice; ServeMux still does all matching, so spec L18 is untouched. Coverage tests assert over the SLICE. 2. TRANSACTIONS: an AST walk over call expressions on `*sql.DB` catching BOTH `BeginTx` and `Begin`, against an explicit allowlist {tx.go, read_tx.go, migrate.go}. 3. SCHEMA: a catalog query over `information_schema` and `pg_constraint` asserting the FK list and each `confdeltype` — version-stable, and it asserts the thing that matters, because the delete actions ARE the delete sheets' copy.

decisions.status: WITHDRAWN in v3, folded into DEC-02
decisions.title: [WITHDRAWN] The `entity_ids` cross-kind uniqueness table and its lifecycle
decisions.evidence: SF8 found two holes in it: nothing removed rows on a cascade delete, and a bare `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` let a trip PUT take an id a city already held — the precise state it existed to refuse.
decisions.reasoning: Both holes were consequences of it being a TABLE. The requirement — an id must be unique across all six kinds — is answered by a six-way `EXISTS` inside the write transaction, which under DEC-06's advisory lock is race-free.
decisions.consequence: No table, no trigger, no lifecycle. The guard SURVIVES as a leg: a trip PUT cannot take an id a city already holds. SF8 is not answered; it is dissolved.

decisions.status: AMENDED IN PLACE at v5 by DEC-49 (V4-SF1); `updated_at` DELETED (over-engineered #3)
decisions.title: Freshness is one integer per traveller, bumped by one line of Go — not by a trigger
decisions.evidence: The cache needs to answer one question: has anything changed since the version I hold? Not 'which rows changed since when'. DEC-25 needed triggers for a specific reason — a per-ROW cursor has to move when an FK-driven `ON DELETE SET NULL` touches a row Go never named, and Go cannot stamp what it does not name.
decisions.reasoning: THAT REASON EVAPORATES FOR A PER-TRAVELLER COUNTER, and the evaporation is worth spelling out because it is why v3 is so much smaller here. A whole-log counter needs only 'a write happened' — and Go always knows that, because Go opens the transaction. Every write goes through `WithTravellerTx`; a cascade inside it is still inside it. So the bump is one statement at the end of the helper, and the six BEFORE UPDATE triggers, the visits-bump-the-parent trigger, the global sequence and the no-op suppression all become unnecessary at once. This is the largest single simplification in v3 and it is a direct consequence of asking a smaller question.
decisions.consequence:
`travellers.logbook_version bigint not null default 0`. `WithTravellerTx` ends with `UPDATE travellers SET logbook_version = logbook_version + 1 WHERE id = $1`, inside the same transaction and under the same advisory lock, so the number and the data commit together. WHICH WRITES BUMP IT IS ENUMERATED IN DEC-50, not implied.

THE ETAG IS `W/"<emitterVersion>-<logbookVersion>"` — DEC-49's form, applied here in place rather than left contradicting it two decisions later. WEAK, because the body bytes are not guaranteed byte-identical across serialisations and a strong ETag would be a claim the server cannot keep. The `emitterVersion` half exists because a DEPLOY that changes the emitted document moves no data and would otherwise leave every cached phone on 304 forever.

THE COST, STATED: one counter means ANY write invalidates the whole cached log. For a single-user app whose writes are a few per session and whose log is 85,422 bytes (85,421 characters) (measured at v5) that is the right trade — it is one integer, it cannot be wrong, and it sees a DELETE for free where `max(updated_at)` cannot. Per-resource ETags are the obvious next step. TRIGGER: a measured complaint about re-fetching, or a log large enough that a full refetch is felt.

`updated_at` IS DELETED FROM EVERY ENTITY TABLE (over-engineered #3). v4 kept it and then had to explain, in a paragraph, that Go sets it, an FK-driven SET NULL does not, and nothing reads it for correctness — a column on six tables, a clause in every UPDATE, and a paragraph existing only so a reader who found the inconsistency would not think an old bug had returned. Deleting the column deletes the need for the paragraph. `created_at` stays; it is read.

decisions.status: NEW in v3
decisions.title: The read path is ONE endpoint, because the log is ~85 KB and the phone already reads it before the first frame
decisions.evidence: TWO measurements, and the second is the one that overturned the brief. (1) The log encodes to 85,422 bytes (85,421 characters) — MEASURED at v5, correcting the 85,422 the client's own record carried. (2) `main.dart` already awaits `openLogbook()` BEFORE `runApp` and hands the result to `logbookSeedProvider`, with the comment at main.dart:20: 'making it async would push an AsyncValue through every one of them for a file read that finishes before the first frame. There is no loading state because there is no frame in which the log is unknown.'
decisions.reasoning: The v3 brief asked for 'read shapes that match screens' and warned about round trips, on the premise that the phone no longer holds everything. It does hold everything — 85 KB is nothing — so the client keeps roughly thirty derivation providers and eighteen screens EXACTLY AS THEY ARE, `logbookProvider` stays synchronous, and no screen grows a loading state. A per-screen endpoint would be a second way to get data the phone already has, and it would force the async rewrite that the whole-log read avoids. Rejecting it is worth days of client work.
decisions.consequence:
`GET /v1/logbook` is the only read. It emits the client's own envelope so `decodeLogbook` parses it unchanged. Conditional: `If-None-Match` against the DEC-30 ETag returns **304 with an empty body**, and THE VERSION LOOKUP HAPPENS FIRST — one indexed SELECT before any other query — so a 304 costs one row read and never assembles the document. A 304 computed after building the body saves bandwidth and no server work, which is half the point and is a leg.

No per-screen reads. No per-resource GETs (`GET /v1/trips/{id}` and friends are CRUD-by-reflex — the whole-log read covers every one of them, and a deep link with a cold cache fetches the log anyway). No search endpoint — Q1 searches the cached document exactly as it does today.

WHERE THIS STOPS BEING TRUE, stated so nobody has to guess: the fat field is `walks.points`, which is unbounded and which almost no screen reads. If the log passes roughly 1 MB, the first thing to split out is points behind its own route — NOT a per-screen BFF. TRIGGER: a measured log over 1 MB, or a cold-start fetch a user can feel.

decisions.status: AMENDED IN PLACE at v5 (V4-SF6) — places is graded by BODY, as cities already was
decisions.title: A write returns what the cache needs, so the phone never issues a second request
decisions.evidence: Under replication the phone already had the answer locally. With the server owning the data, a write that returns nothing leaves the cache stale and forces a follow-up `GET /v1/logbook` — doubling every write's round trips on exactly the path that is now blocking on the network.
decisions.reasoning: A flat rule 'always return the whole log' is simple but sends ~85 KB back for a caption edit. A flat rule 'always return the entity' is small but wrong for a cascade, whose effect is unbounded — `DELETE /v1/trips/{id}` can remove hundreds of photographs and shorten several places' visit arrays, and no bounded response describes that. So the rule is GRADED, and it has an exception because the exception is real.
decisions.consequence:
EVERY write response carries the new `ETag`, always. Then:
- Non-cascading create/update (`PUT` on trips, cities, places, photos, walks; the three share routes; `PATCH /v1/me`) -> **200 + the affected entity**.
- Non-cascading delete (`DELETE /v1/photos/{id}` — nothing in the log points at a photo) -> **204 + ETag**, no body.
- Cascading write (`DELETE /v1/trips/{id}`, `DELETE /v1/places/{id}` in either branch, `POST /refile`, `PUT /v1/cities/{id}` with `attachTo`) -> **200 + THE WHOLE LOGBOOK DOCUMENT + ETag**. The phone would have had to re-fetch anyway, so returning it IS the refresh, folded into the same round trip.
Smoke asserts the cascade case end to end: `DELETE` a trip and see the wishlist place SURVIVING in that same response body — one request proving both the cascade and the cache contract.

`PUT /v1/places/{id}` IS GRADED BY BODY, NOT BY ROUTE — the treatment cities already had and places did not. The PUT carries the whole ordered visits array, and `photos.visit_id -> visits ON DELETE SET NULL` means a body that DROPS a visit any photograph references silently clears that reference. A phone told the write was non-cascading splices the place and keeps photographs pointing at a visit that is gone. RULE: a visits array that drops a visit referenced by a photograph is REFUSED — `422 invalid_field, field=visits` — rather than accepted and re-graded, because no client action shrinks a visits array today and a refusal is the honest answer to a body no caller should be sending. If one ever should, it becomes cascading and returns the whole logbook. LEG: a PUT dropping a referenced visit is refused; a PUT dropping an unreferenced one succeeds.

decisions.status: NEW in v3, replacing DEC-07 and DEC-22
decisions.title: No idempotency apparatus, because every verb is already idempotent by construction
decisions.evidence: THE CLIENT MINTS EVERY ID. `PUT /v1/trips/{id}` and every sibling are upserts on a client-supplied key. `DELETE` answers 204 on an unknown id by the client's own asymmetry, so a repeat is a success that writes nothing. `POST /v1/photos/{id}/refile` carries the client-minted `visitId` (SF4). `POST /v1/trips/{id}/share` carries the client-minted token (DEC-10). v2's last surviving argument for a universal key was that a retry racing a TOMBSTONE answers 409 where the original answered 200 — and tombstones are gone.
decisions.reasoning: An idempotency table, a fingerprint, a replay path, a response-size cap and two error codes existed to make retries safe. Retries are already safe. Keeping the apparatus would be carrying a mechanism whose entire justification has been withdrawn — which is exactly the kind of thing that survives a reversal by inertia and then confuses everyone who reads it.
decisions.consequence: No `Idempotency-Key` header, no table, no middleware. THE ONE EXCEPTION, NAMED RATHER THAN IGNORED: `POST /v1/auth/session` mints a new session on every call, so a retried login leaves two valid sessions. That is harmless (both expire, either can be revoked) and it is the only non-idempotent verb in the API. THE TRIGGER THAT WOULD BRING THE APPARATUS BACK: any endpoint where the SERVER mints an id the client cannot supply. DEC-38 introduces exactly such an id — a media object id — and content-addressing is precisely how it stays idempotent without one; if that ever became a random id, this decision reopens.

decisions.status: NEW in v3
decisions.title: The cache policy: what the phone keeps, what invalidates it, what clears it
decisions.evidence: The client already has the mechanism — `logbook_store.dart` writes and reads one JSON document in the app documents directory, and `main.dart` reads it before the first frame. What changes is its STATUS: it was the record, it is now a cache.
decisions.reasoning: Stating the policy is the difference between a cache and an accident. The client's existing store is reused rather than replaced, which is why this costs so little.
decisions.consequence:
KEEPS: the whole logbook document plus its ETag, in the app documents directory — the same file `logbook_store.dart` already writes. Photograph BYTES are a separate cache keyed by object id (DEC-38), size-bounded and evicted, and the client already has the precedent — `flutter_map`'s tile cache with a 150 MB ceiling under the platform CACHE directory, which is where photograph bytes belong for the same reason: losing them costs bandwidth, not data.
INVALIDATED BY: any write response's new ETag — and because DEC-32 makes writes return enough to rebuild, invalidation is usually a REPLACEMENT rather than a fetch. Otherwise by a 200 (not 304) on the next conditional request.
REFRESHED: once after the first frame, and on resume. Never before the first frame — that is what keeps `logbookProvider` synchronous.
CLEARED BY: logout, which must delete the cache file and the byte cache. NOTE the exposure this creates and that the client already made: phase 6 set `UIFileSharingEnabled` and `LSSupportsOpeningDocumentsInPlace`, so the documents directory is visible in Files.app. The cache is the traveller's data sitting somewhere anyone holding the phone can read, which was already true of the log and is not a regression — but a SESSION TOKEN must not join it. See CLIENT-PREREQUISITES.
A CORRUPT CACHE IS DELETED AND RE-FETCHED, not quarantined. Nothing is lost, so the sidecar, S1's notice and U2's sidecar export line all become unnecessary — a simplification AVAILABLE to the client, not required by this plan.

decisions.status: AMENDED in v4 (V3-SF3) — the attribution was wrong and it is now four sentences
decisions.title: Writes are blocked with no signal, and D1's sentence stops being truthful
decisions.evidence: The human's ruling: reads work from the cache, writes are BLOCKED with a clear reason, no queue and no deferred writes. And the client's D1 copy, verbatim: 'Your log could not be saved, so nothing was deleted. The photograph is still here.'
decisions.reasoning:
THE SERVER'S HALF IS NOTHING — a blocked write is a request never made, and there is no offline endpoint to design. THE CLIENT'S HALF IS A COPY PROBLEM, and it is sharper than 'add an offline state'. When the save was a local file write, 'nothing was deleted' was a guarantee: the write either landed or it did not, and the app knew which. When the save is a network call, a lost RESPONSE is indistinguishable from a lost REQUEST — the delete may well have succeeded on the server. The sentence is then a confident claim the app cannot back.
WHAT MAKES IT TRACTABLE IS DEC-33: because every verb is idempotent, the client can safely RETRY and then re-read, and arrive at the truth rather than guessing at it. So the honest client behaviour is retry-then-refresh, and the copy needs to cover a genuinely-unknown interval rather than assert an outcome.
decisions.consequence:
THIS IS DESIGN WORK, NOT A CODE CHANGE, and it is flagged as such in CLIENT-PREREQUISITES.md. FOUR sentences are affected — v3 said three and misfiled the fourth.
1. D1, `delete_sheets.dart:165` — 'Your log could not be saved, so nothing was deleted. The photograph is still here.'
2. D2, `delete_sheets.dart:367` — 'so nothing was removed'.
3. H1, `share_sheet_screen.dart:240-241` — 'Your log could not be saved, so nothing changed. What the link carries is what it carried before.'
4. D3, `delete_sheets.dart:650` — 'The shared link stops working'. CORRECTED IN v4: v3 attributed this to H1. It is D3's, inside `if (trip.isShared)` in the trip-DELETE sheet, and `grep -rn 'stops working' lib/src/screens/` returns that line and nothing else. H1 has no such sentence, so a designer briefed by v3 would have opened H1, found nothing, and left the promise standing — on the sheet where the user is typing a trip's name to destroy it, which is the most consequential surface in the app.

The first three assert an OUTCOME a network write cannot guarantee: a lost response is indistinguishable from a lost request, so the delete may well have succeeded. What makes them tractable is DEC-33 — every verb is idempotent, so the client can safely RETRY and then re-read, and arrive at the truth rather than guessing. The honest behaviour is retry-then-refresh and the copy must cover a genuinely unknown interval.
The FOURTH is a different problem: it promises revocation, and under DEC-47 an already-minted photograph URL keeps working until the PUBLIC presign TTL expires. D3's copy must be written against `S3_PRESIGN_TTL_PUBLIC` — the honest revocation window — and not against the short private one. DEC-44 rules that H1's wording is adjusted so the screen does not overstate; D3's line needs the same pass, and it is the same pass.

The design system has no toast and refuses one, so the replacement goes where the failure already goes — the liveRegion line the sheet already has. The plan does not write the copy; it names the constraint precisely so whoever does is not guessing.

decisions.status: AMENDED in v4 — the hand-rolled presigner is WITHDRAWN by DEC-43
decisions.title: HALF TWO: photographs go to S3-compatible object storage, uploaded DIRECT by presigned PUT
decisions.evidence: Ruled by the human: photographs go to S3-compatible object storage, uploaded separately from the JSON API — upload bytes, get an id, set the id on the `Photo`. Photographs are megabytes each; the log is ~85 KB. They are not the same problem and must not share a mechanism.
decisions.reasoning:
WHY NOT POSTGRES: bytea puts megabytes into the row store, bloats every backup, and routes image reads through the connection pool — the same pool already sized against Argon2's 64 MiB-per-login ceiling. WHY DIRECT UPLOAD RATHER THAN PROXIED THROUGH GO: a proxied upload occupies an HTTP handler for megabytes the API has no reason to touch, and that is exactly the contention the pool sizing exists to avoid. A presigned PUT means the API handles two small JSON requests per upload and never sees a byte.

WHAT v3 GOT WRONG HERE, struck rather than quietly replaced: v3 ruled the signing HAND-ROLLED over crypto/hmac, ~150 lines, with minio-go named only as a fallback. DEC-43 reverses that, and the reason is one v3 did not weigh — SIGNING IS THE ONE PLACE A BUG PASSES LOCALLY AND FAILS IN PRODUCTION. MinIO is a more forgiving verifier than real S3, so a hand-rolled canonical request can look correct for the whole of development. v3's own mitigation ('a wrong signature 403s LOUDLY') assumed the verifier that would do the 403ing was the one in production, and in the local stack it is not.
decisions.consequence:
`internal/objects` holds a `Store` interface — PresignGet, PresignPut, Head, Delete, and (DEC-47) a batch mint — with ONE thin minio-go implementation and one in-memory implementation for handler tests. Endpoint, bucket, region and credentials come from env, so MinIO locally and real S3 or R2 in production is configuration, not code.

MEASURED BEFORE ADOPTING, because this exact class already bit once with x/crypto: minio-go v7.3.0 declares EXACTLY `go 1.25.0`, tidy leaves the directive alone, and build and vet both exit 0. It brings 18 indirect modules — the largest dependency footprint in the project — and `golang.org/x/crypto` is now among them, which OVERTAKES DEC-08's cost arithmetic and makes Argon2id strictly cheaper than when it was ruled on. DEC-27's floor is now forced independently by two dependencies rather than one. This is the THIRD dependency conversation after the original six and Argon2id, and it is recorded as a first-class decision rather than as a fallback with a trigger.
decisions.commit_note: S11's commit message must not say 'SigV4 over crypto/hmac'; that deliverable no longer exists.

decisions.status: AMENDED in v4 (V3-SF1) — its stated reasoning was measured FALSE; the decision survives on its second, independent leg
decisions.title: Presigned URLs never appear in the log payload, or the cache is dead while appearing to work
decisions.evidence: A presigned URL contains an expiry and a signature, so it DIFFERS ON EVERY MINT. Put one in `GET /v1/logbook` and the body changes on every request; the DEC-30 ETag would have to change with it or lie; `If-None-Match` never matches; `304` never fires; and every app open re-downloads the whole log. NOTHING WOULD LOOK BROKEN — the app would work, just slowly and expensively, and the 304 leg would still pass if it were written against a log with no photographs in it.
decisions.reasoning:
The resolution is to keep the two things apart rather than reconcile them. The log carries the OPAQUE OBJECT ID in `Photo.asset` and nothing else, so the payload is a pure function of the data and is stable. Bytes are reached through a separate route, and THE PHONE CACHES BYTES KEYED BY OBJECT ID, so an expired URL never invalidates a cached image — the URL is a delivery detail with a short life, the id is the identity and is forever.

THE ROUTE SHAPE, WITH v3's FIRST REASON STRUCK. v3 rejected a `302` redirect because Dart's `HttpClient` would re-issue the request with its original headers and leak a Bearer token to the bucket. MEASURED FALSE at http_impl.dart:3072-3089 — `shouldCopyHeaderOnRedirect` refuses `authorization`, `www-authenticate`, `proxy-authorization`, `proxy-authenticate`, `cookie` and `cookie2` unless the redirect is same-origin. That leak could not have happened. THE DECISION STANDS ON ITS SECOND, INDEPENDENT LEG: the phone needs a disk byte cache keyed by object id and therefore a custom `ImageProvider` regardless (Flutter's `ImageCache` is memory-only, and DEC-47 has now promoted that from a note to a REQUIRED client item), so the redirect's only advantage — 'it works with a plain image widget' — never existed either.

AND THE NUANCE WORTH KEEPING, which is the useful half of the wrong claim: NON-sensitive headers ARE copied cross-origin. So the leak v3 described would be REAL for a custom header like `X-Auth-Token`. That is a positive argument for holding the credential in `Authorization` and never inventing a bespoke auth header, and it goes in CLAUDE.md as such.
decisions.consequence:
`POST /v1/media/mint` -> `200 {"urls": [{"id":..., "url":..., "expiresAt":...}]}`, authenticated, taking a LIST of ids, and the client fetches each URL unauthenticated. THE SINGULAR `GET /v1/media/{id}` IS DELETED (over-engineered #1): it is the batch with a one-element list — same auth, same capability headers, same TTL, same payload — and it cost a second handler, a second set of `no-store` legs, a second route-coverage entry and a second place to get the private-vs-public TTL wrong. No credential ever reaches the storage host. `expiresAt` lets the phone hold a URL for its lifetime instead of re-minting per retry.
PRESIGN LIFETIME: 15 minutes, from config, UNTUNED (DEC-21). IT IS THE REVOCATION KNOB AND THE TRADE IS EXPLICIT: 'Stop sharing' stops new URLs being minted immediately, but a URL already handed out keeps working until it expires. SO REVOCATION OF THE BYTES IS BOUNDED, NOT INSTANT. Shorter expiry tightens the window and costs more re-mints. The only designs that give instant revocation are proxying bytes through Go (rejected above) or rotating bucket credentials (nuclear). This is stated here, and its copy consequence for H1 is stated in DEC-35.
AND THE ASYMMETRY THAT LOOKS INCONSISTENT AND IS DELIBERATE: the PUBLIC envelope (DEC-24) DOES embed presigned URLs, because it has no cache contract to break — a browser fetching a share page benefits from one round trip, and if the page outlives the expiry it re-fetches the envelope, which is what a refresh is. The log payload is cacheable and must not carry URLs; the public envelope is not cached and may. Written down because otherwise it reads as a mistake.

decisions.status: AMENDED in v4 — four fixes: the upsert, the bucket key, the liveness columns, and where `immutable` actually comes from
decisions.title: The object id is a SHA-256 content hash, and one sweep solves orphans and detached objects together
decisions.evidence: The fixture cycles TWO bundled PNGs across every photograph, so content addressing stores two objects where a random id would store one per photo. And DEC-33's guarantee — every verb idempotent because the client mints every id — is BROKEN by an id the server mints at upload: a retried upload with a random id creates a second object nobody references.
decisions.reasoning:
Content addressing restores idempotency for the one operation that would otherwise lose it (same bytes, same id, same object, retry is free), dedupes, and makes `Cache-Control: immutable` HONEST rather than optimistic — the bytes at an id can never change, so the phone never revalidates an image it already holds and eviction becomes purely a size decision. A random id gives none of that and buys only simpler deletion.
THE SERVER MUST NOT TRUST THE CLIENT'S HASH, or a lying client poisons the address space. The presigned PUT is signed REQUIRING an `x-amz-checksum-sha256` header matching the claimed digest [assumed — verify MinIO honours it], so the STORAGE LAYER rejects mismatched bytes and the API never downloads anything to verify.
DELETION IS WHERE CONTENT ADDRESSING COSTS SOMETHING: two Photos can share bytes, so deleting one must not delete the object. That is a refcount — and the same query answers the orphan question the brief raised, so it is one mechanism rather than two.
decisions.consequence:
THREE MEDIA ROUTES:
1. `POST /v1/media` — `{sha256, byteSize, contentType}` -> `{id, uploadUrl, expiresAt, alreadyExists}`. `alreadyExists: true` means SKIP THE UPLOAD ENTIRELY; it is what makes the fixture cost two uploads instead of N, and it is a leg.
2. `POST /v1/media/{id}/commit` — the server HEADs the bucket, verifies the object exists and the size matches, and sets `uploaded_at`. `409 {"code":"upload_incomplete"}` when it does not. Without this the server never learns an upload succeeded and a `Photo` could reference a broken image.
3. `POST /v1/media/mint` — DEC-37's read mint, taking a LIST of ids. (The singular `GET /v1/media/{id}` was DELETED as over-engineered #1: it is this route with a one-element list.)
`media_objects(traveller_id, id text, byte_size, content_type, created_at, uploaded_at null)`. `PUT /v1/photos/{id}` REJECTS an `asset` that is not a committed object for that traveller — `422 invalid_field, field=asset`. SINCE DEC-58 THIS IS ENFORCED TWICE, DELIBERATELY: in Go for the message, and in the SCHEMA as the guarantee. The Go check is not the guard and must not be deleted as redundant.
ORPHANS AND DETACHED OBJECTS, ONE RULE: an object is live iff some photo's `asset` equals its id. A `-sweep-media` flag on the binary deletes objects that are unreferenced AND older than a 24-hour grace window — the grace is what stops it deleting an object uploaded seconds before its Photo lands. That covers never-attached (orphan) and once-attached-now-deleted (detached) with one query. NO SCHEDULER IS BUILT: the flag is run by hand or by cron later, and until it runs, orphans cost bytes and not correctness. Stated in BEFORE-A-PUBLIC-DEPLOY.md. THIS IS THE ONLY SWEEP IN v3 and it is not DEC-22 returning — different mechanism, different problem.

=== v4 AMENDMENTS ===
THE BEGIN ROUTE MUST UPSERT (V3-B5). v3 described begin as 'dedupe check, presigned PUT, alreadyExists' — a SELECT-then-INSERT. Two concurrent begins for the same bytes (which is EXACTLY the retry this design exists to make free) both miss the SELECT and the second INSERT raises a unique violation on `(traveller_id, id)`. The one operation the plan singles out as idempotent was the one that was not, under concurrency. Fix: `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (traveller_id, id) DO UPDATE SET byte_size = EXCLUDED.byte_size WHERE media_objects.uploaded_at IS NULL`, inside the traveller lock — and `alreadyExists` is derived from `uploaded_at IS NOT NULL`, NOT from row presence, or a begin that never uploaded reports `alreadyExists: true`, the client skips an upload that never happened, and commit 409s with no way forward.

THE BUCKET KEY IS `<traveller_uuid>/<sha256>` (V3-SF9). The database row is keyed `(traveller_id, id)` but v3 never said what the BUCKET key was. A bare hash means two travellers with identical bytes share one object while each holds a row, so `-sweep-media` evaluated per traveller deletes an object the other still references — one traveller's sweep breaks another's photographs — and `alreadyExists` computed from the bucket becomes a cross-tenant confirmation oracle over known images. Both are defused TODAY only because `POST /v1/auth/register` answers 409 when a traveller exists, and relying on that is exactly the kind of load-bearing accident this plan writes down. Prefixing costs one cross-traveller dedupe nobody wants. TRIGGER: the day a second traveller can register, a bare-hash key becomes a cross-tenant delete.

LIVENESS IS FOUR COLUMNS, NOT ONE (V3-B6, ruled by DEC-46). `photos.asset`, `trips.coverAsset`, `cities.coverAsset`, `places.coverAsset`. With one column the sweep deletes objects that are live and every cover in the log breaks with no way to recover the bytes. A leg asserts a cover-only object survives the sweep, and its mutation proof narrows the query back to one column.

WHERE `Cache-Control: immutable` COMES FROM, AND WHAT IT IS ACTUALLY FOR (V3-SF11). With a direct-to-bucket PUT the API never touches the response headers, so the header must be `response-cache-control` on the PRESIGNED GET — the one mechanism that does not depend on the uploader having sent it. And the honest statement of its value: an HTTP cache keys on URL, every mint is a NEW url, so `immutable` buys the PHONE nothing. It is for intermediaries. THE PHONE'S CORRECTNESS COMES ENTIRELY FROM ITS OWN BYTE CACHE KEYED BY OBJECT ID. v3 implied two mechanisms where there is one, and saying so is the difference between a design and a decoration.

=== v5 AMENDMENTS, APPLIED TO THE ROUTES THEMSELVES ===
TWO ENCODINGS OF ONE DIGEST, AND THEY WERE NEVER DISTINGUISHED (V4-SF4). The object id, `sha256Re`, the `media_objects` CHECK and the bucket key all carry the digest as **hex** (64 chars). The signed `x-amz-checksum-sha256` header value is the **base64** of the same raw 32 bytes (44 chars). A worker who signs the hex string gets a rejection on every upload. This fails CLOSED, so it is not the fail-open class — but it lands in the one line the plan flags as unforgiving, so it is stated there and asserted in the integration leg.
BEGIN MUST NOT HAND OUT A WRITE CAPABILITY FOR A COMMITTED OBJECT (V4-SF5a). `alreadyExists: true` means skip the upload, so the response OMITS `uploadUrl` entirely — a leg asserts the key is ABSENT, not empty. DEC-24 already made this exact call correctly for the public envelope ('no URL is minted at all — not an unusable one, not an expired one'); the same rule belongs here, and handing out a live write URL against an object being served `immutable` is worse than a merely redundant one.
THE UPSERT MUST NOT REWRITE A COMMITTED ROW (V4-SF5b): `DO UPDATE SET byte_size = EXCLUDED.byte_size WHERE media_objects.uploaded_at IS NULL`. Without the guard a re-begin with a false `byteSize` rewrites the recorded size of an object whose bytes cannot change, leaving row and bucket disagreeing with nothing able to detect it.
NO `RETURNING` PROJECTION (over-engineered #4, deleted at v5). v4 carried `RETURNING (xmax = 0) AS inserted`, which returned a value nothing consumed — `alreadyExists` is derived from `uploaded_at IS NOT NULL`, which is the correction that made the fix right. It survived from the shape of the problem rather than the shape of the answer.

decisions.status: AMENDED in v4 — DEC-46 makes it four fields, and DEC-53 gives the rule a mechanism
decisions.title: `logbookFormatVersion` moves to 2 — cheap now, and a CACHE makes format refusal WORSE than a record did
decisions.evidence: `Photo.asset` changes MEANING: a bundled asset path becomes an opaque object id. The client's own rule: 'Move the version when an old file's *meaning* changes, and write the migration in the same commit.' A build reading the wrong version would construct `AssetImage('ab12cd...')` and fail, or treat a bundle path as an object id and 404.
decisions.reasoning:
THE COST OF A BUMP COLLAPSED, because the local file is a cache and not a record: an unreadable cache is discarded and re-fetched, where an unreadable record was quarantined and the user lost everything. So the bump is warranted and nearly free.
BUT — AND THIS IS THE FINDING — A CACHE MAKES FORMAT REFUSAL WORSE IN ONE SPECIFIC WAY, and neither brief carried it. Under the record model, an old build meeting a new file quarantined it and STOPPED: bad, but terminal and visible. Under the cache model, an old build meeting a new server discards the cache, re-fetches, receives the SAME rejected version, discards again — a permanent refetch loop, and the app is bricked rather than merely stuck, silently, and it burns data doing it. Format refusal is safe when the source is a file you can leave alone and dangerous when the source is a server that keeps answering.
WHY IT COSTS NOTHING TODAY: nothing has shipped against this backend. There is no installed base, so the server emits 2 from day one and the client is changed in the same phase to expect 2. No migration, no negotiation, no loop.
decisions.consequence:
The server emits `"version": 2`. The client's `logbookFormatVersion` becomes 2 in the same phase — a CLIENT-PREREQUISITES entry, because a server emitting 2 to a client expecting 1 is the loop above.
THE RULE FOR NEXT TIME, recorded in CLAUDE.md because it changes the moment the client ships: once a client build exists in the world, a MEANING change goes in the PATH (`/v2/logbook`), not in the payload version. An old client then gets a clean 404 or 410 and can say so, instead of looping. The payload version stays for ADDITIVE changes only, which is what DEC-13 always said it was for.
AND ONE THING THE BUMP DOES NOT NEED: a migration. There is no v1 file anywhere to migrate.

=== v4 AMENDMENTS ===
THE BUMP DESCRIBES FOUR FIELDS, NOT ONE (DEC-46). `Photo.asset`, `Trip.coverAsset`, `City.coverAsset` and `Place.coverAsset` all change meaning from a bundle path to an object id. v3 cited only the first, from which a reader would conclude covers stay bundle paths — and nothing said so, nothing validated it, and S14's PUT would have accepted whatever the client sent. One field carrying two meanings is how a cleanup job deletes live data.

AND THE RULE NOW HAS A MECHANISM (V3-SF8). v3's 'server and client move to 2 together, and afterwards a meaning change goes in the PATH' was a scheduling promise, and nothing made the loop impossible if the premise failed — a rollback, a phone that missed an update. DEC-53 is the mechanism.

decisions.status: NEW in v3 — RULED: defer the decision, never the seam
decisions.title: The bucket's public base address is a config value from the first commit that signs anything
decisions.evidence: A SigV4 signature COVERS THE HOST. A presigned URL minted against `http://minio:9000` is valid only for that host: a proxy cannot rewrite it, a `Host` header cannot correct it, and a CNAME cannot rescue it — the signature simply fails. So an address baked into signing code is not a value that can be changed downstream; it is a value that can only be changed by editing code and re-testing every signed URL.
decisions.reasoning:
Two related questions are deliberately DEFERRED to the infrastructure steps (see `deferred_decisions`): which hostname a physical iPhone uses to reach the local stack, and which hostname the bucket is addressed by. Deferring them is right — they depend on a LAN, a certificate story and a device nobody has plugged in yet. But deferring the DECISION only stays cheap if the SEAM exists now. Otherwise S22 stops being an infrastructure step and becomes a code change with a signing re-test attached, which is exactly the late surprise this plan is written to avoid.
THIS IS THE HOUSE STYLE AND A WORKER WILL RECOGNISE IT. The client makes the same argument twice: `mapTileSourceProvider` is one provider precisely so swapping OSM for a keyed basemap is one line, and `apiBaseUrlProvider` THROWS until it is overridden rather than carrying a placeholder — 'a placeholder host would fail later as a connection error, so this throws immediately instead'. The seam exists so the choice stays cheap, and an unconfigured seam fails loudly rather than plausibly.
decisions.consequence:
TWO environment variables from the first commit that touches object storage (S11), both read in `internal/config` and NOWHERE else:
- `S3_PUBLIC_BASE_URL` — the address the CLIENT will reach media at. THE SIGNER TAKES THIS ONE, always, for both presigned GET and presigned PUT, because it is the host the phone and the browser will actually connect to.
- `S3_INTERNAL_ENDPOINT` — the address the API itself uses for HEAD and DELETE from inside the Compose network. Defaults to the public one when unset, because they are the same thing in every deployment except a containerised local stack.
NEITHER HAS A HARDCODED FALLBACK and neither may appear as a literal in a signing call — an acceptance check greps that `minio`, `9000` and any `http://` literal appear nowhere under `internal/objects`. Both join the `.env.example` coverage test that S23 specifies — the test that PARSES both files rather than reading them — so the pair cannot go stale the first time a third address is added.
WHAT THIS BUYS: S22 changing the media address is one line in `.env`. Without it, S22 is a code edit plus a re-run of every presign leg.

decisions.title: RULED — two presign lifetimes: a short private one that is the revocation knob, a longer public one that is the honest revocation window (V3-SF2)
decisions.evidence: DEC-44's two minutes is right for the phone, which re-fetches constantly and caches bytes by object id. It is wrong for `GET /l/{token}`, which embeds URLs directly in a document with nothing to re-mint them: a viewer who scrolls or leaves a tab gets 403s below the fold, and v3's stated recovery ('the page re-fetches the envelope, which is what a refresh is') describes a behaviour nothing implements, because the plan builds no page.
decisions.reasoning: One knob cannot serve a client that re-mints cheaply and a document that cannot re-mint at all.
decisions.consequence:
`S3_PRESIGN_TTL_PRIVATE` (short — the revocation knob, the phone's path) and `S3_PRESIGN_TTL_PUBLIC` (long enough for a page to be read). THE PUBLIC ONE IS WHAT D3's AND H1's COPY IS WRITTEN AGAINST — not the private one, and DEC-35 says so where the designer will read it.

(b) 'An `ImageProvider` keyed by OBJECT ID' is PROMOTED in CLIENT-PREREQUISITES from a note to a REQUIRED item, with the reason attached: `NetworkImage`'s equality is `(url, scale)`, so every re-mint is a different cache key and Flutter's in-memory `ImageCache` misses every time. Under a short TTL that is not an optimisation, it is the difference between a working image grid and a re-download on every scroll.

decisions.status: RULED 22 Aug 2026
decisions.title: RULED — the auth routes get a rate limit and an Argon2 concurrency cap in v1, at S10 (V3-B13)
decisions.evidence: The plan states the 64 MiB-per-login cost THREE times — 'a memory ceiling per concurrent login', 'it competes with DB_MAX_OPEN_CONNS for the same RAM', 'direct-to-bucket upload exists partly so multi-megabyte transfers never join that contest' — and then leaves `POST /v1/auth/session` and `POST /v1/auth/register` with no limit at all. The only limiter in v3 was on the public read. Thirty-two concurrent unauthenticated POSTs is 2 GiB of Argon2 memory on the box whose pool the plan sized so carefully.
decisions.reasoning: The plan reasoned its way to the danger and then guarded the wrong route. It is roughly ten lines, and the limiter and the client-IP resolution both already exist by S10. 'We will add the rate limit before we deploy' is the sentence that is true right up until it is not.
decisions.consequence: `AUTH_RATE_LIMIT_PER_MIN` per client address on register and session, plus a buffered-channel semaphore capping concurrent `argon2.IDKey` calls at a configured number. REJECT WITH `429 {"code":"rate_limited"}` RATHER THAN QUEUEING — queueing converts memory exhaustion into timeout exhaustion, which is the same outage wearing a different error. One leg: the N+1th concurrent login is REFUSED, not made to wait. This turns the plan's most-repeated measurement from a documented ceiling into an enforced one.

decisions.status: NEW in v4 — V3-B3, and it is a harder brick than the one v3 caught
decisions.title: The ETag covers the emitter as well as the data, and it dies with the document it validates
decisions.evidence: TWO defects in v3's centre of gravity. (a) `W/"<logbook_version>"` moves only on a WRITE. A deploy that changes the emitted document — a field added, a date rendered differently, DEC-40's `"version": 2` itself — does not move it, so every phone holding a cached body gets 304 forever and keeps serving the OLD SHAPE until somebody happens to write. The validator did not cover the thing that produced the bytes. (b) DEC-34 said the cache holds 'the whole logbook document plus its ETag' and separately that a corrupt cache is 'DELETED AND RE-FETCHED'. It never said the ETag dies WITH the document. Discard the file, keep the ETag, re-fetch: 304 WITH AN EMPTY BODY. The phone now has no log and no way to get one, permanently and silently.
decisions.reasoning: (b) is worse than the DEC-40 refetch loop v3 did catch: the loop at least burns visibly, and this ends in a quiet, permanent empty app. Both defects are the same root — v3 treated the ETag as a fact about the database when it is a claim about a RESPONSE, which is a function of the data AND the code that rendered it AND the cache entry it belongs to.
decisions.consequence:
THE ETAG IS `W/"<emitterVersion>-<logbookVersion>"`. `emitterVersion` is a Go constant, bumped BY HAND whenever the emitter changes shape, sitting immediately above the emitter with a comment saying what it is for. A leg asserts the constant appears in the emitted ETag, so it cannot be quietly dropped; and DEC-40's move to `"version": 2` is itself the first bump, which is the worked example.
AND THE LIFECYCLE INVARIANT, written into CACHE-POLICY.md as the client-side rule it is: THE ETAG IS STORED INSIDE THE CACHE DOCUMENT AND IS DISCARDED WITH IT — never stored separately, never kept across a discard, never written before the body it describes. A client leg later, and a sentence in CLIENT-PREREQUISITES now.

decisions.status: NEW in v4 — V3-B4, and both obvious answers were wrong
decisions.title: Two transaction helpers, and the two lists of what uses each are enumerated rather than implied
decisions.evidence: DEC-30's mechanism is 'every write goes through `WithTravellerTx`, which ends with the counter bump'. Two write classes are not logbook writes, v3 never said which side of the line they fell on, and BOTH answers were broken. (a) SESSIONS: S08 gives them `last_used_at`, implying a write on every authenticated request. Through `WithTravellerTx` that invalidates the phone's whole ~85 KB cache on EVERY REQUEST — the cache would never once hit 304 in real use. AND THE 304 LEG WOULD STILL PASS, because it never authenticates twice. (b) MEDIA inserts: not in the logbook payload, so bumping is a whole-log invalidation per upload — but going OUTSIDE the helper loses the advisory lock that DEC-02's six-way EXISTS and DEC-38's begin-upsert BOTH declare themselves race-free under.
decisions.reasoning: The helper was doing two jobs — take the lock, and bump the counter — and the two jobs have different memberships. Splitting them is smaller than any rule about when to skip the bump.
decisions.consequence:
`WithTravellerTx` = advisory lock + counter bump. `WithTravellerLock` = advisory lock, no bump. BOTH LISTS ARE ENUMERATED IN CLAUDE.md AT S08 AND ARE THE SPEC:
- BUMPS (WithTravellerTx): trips, cities, places, visits, photos, walks, share_links, traveller name. Everything in the logbook payload.
- DOES NOT BUMP (WithTravellerLock): sessions (create, `last_used_at`, revoke) and media_objects (begin, commit, sweep). Nothing in the payload.
NEITHER HELPER — `POST /v1/auth/register`, which INSERTs the traveller row. It cannot take a per-traveller advisory lock on a traveller that does not exist yet, so it goes through neither, which is correct and was unstated in a decision whose own text says 'BOTH LISTS ARE ENUMERATED AND ARE THE SPEC'. It is the ONLY write outside both helpers, and S08's AST check allowlists it EXPLICITLY rather than leaving it as the one exception a worker discovers.
THE LEG THAT CATCHES (a) AND DID NOT EXIST: authenticate, GET (200 + ETag), AUTHENTICATE AGAIN so `last_used_at` is genuinely written, GET with If-None-Match, assert 304. Its absence is precisely why the defect was invisible. Mutation proof: route the session update through `WithTravellerTx` and watch it redden.

decisions.status: NEW in v4 — V3-B11 and V3-B12
decisions.title: The capability surface is hardened: no-store, no-referrer, a content-type allowlist and a signed size bound
decisions.evidence: MEASURED against v3's own text: `Cache-Control` appeared ONCE (about object immutability) and `no-store` appeared ZERO times. So `GET /l/{token}` — a JSON document containing LIVE MEDIA CAPABILITIES — was cacheable by any intermediary and by the browser's back-forward cache, and after 'Stop sharing' a viewer or a shared proxy could re-read the URLs and keep fetching for as long as the cached envelope survived. That is NOT bounded by the presign lifetime, which unbounds the very window DEC-44 shrank. Separately, `POST /v1/media` took `{sha256, byteSize, contentType}` with no allowlist, no bound and no disposition: an object stored as `text/html` is served AS HTML FROM THE BUCKET ORIGIN, at a URL the public share envelope embeds.
decisions.reasoning: v3's 'the public envelope has no cache contract to break' is true of the SERVER's contract and false of every cache between the server and the viewer. And `payload_too_large` was applied only to the 1 MiB JSON reader, while the presigned PUT bound no `content-length` at all — so anyone holding an upload URL could write an object of arbitrary size.
decisions.consequence:
ON RESPONSES CARRYING CAPABILITIES — `GET /l/{token}` and `POST /v1/media/mint`: `Cache-Control: no-store, private` and `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer` (without which the bucket URL travels in a Referer header to any origin the page later reaches). A leg asserts the headers; the mutation proof removes them.
ON WHAT MAY BE STORED: `contentTypeRe = ^image/(jpeg|png|heic)$` with a `422 invalid_field, field=contentType` leg; `byteSize` bounded by `MEDIA_MAX_BYTES` from config; and `content-length` SIGNED INTO the presigned PUT so the BUCKET enforces it rather than the API hoping. `response-content-disposition: attachment` on the presigned GET, so a mislabelled object is downloaded rather than rendered on the storage origin. `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` IS STRUCK (V4-SF3): S3's response-header override set is CLOSED — content-type, -language, -expires, -cache-control, -disposition, -encoding — and nosniff is neither in it nor a storable system header, so no presigned GET can produce it. minio-go does not validate reqParams, so an invented `response-x-...` would be signed happily and surface as a 400 or a silently absent header, and a leg asserting it could never pass. THE DEFENCE IS THE DISPOSITION PLUS THE `^image/(jpeg|png|heic)$` ALLOWLIST, and the residual is named: a mislabelled object is downloaded, never rendered. Real nosniff needs a proxy in front of the bucket, which is a different decision.
Single-traveller registration bounds who can upload TODAY. The public envelope exists precisely so untrusted parties fetch those URLs, so that bound is not the guard.

decisions.status: AMENDED IN PLACE at v5 (V4-B6) — the first fixture is GENERATED, not copied, and it now exists

decisions.status: NEW in v4 — V3-SF8, giving DEC-40's rule a mechanism instead of a promise
decisions.title: The client declares the format version it can read, and the server refuses in a way the client can act on
decisions.evidence: DEC-40's analysis was the best new finding in v3 and its fix was a scheduling promise: server and client 'move to 2 together in one phase', and afterwards 'a meaning change goes in the PATH'. Nothing made the loop impossible if the premise failed — a server rollback, a phone that missed an update, a `/v1` path serving a payload version the client refuses. The client's decoder throws on an unknown version, and under the cache model that means discard, re-fetch, receive the same refusal, forever.
decisions.reasoning: Cheap now, while it costs nothing and there is no installed base to negotiate with. A promise about future scheduling is not a mechanism, and the whole point of DEC-40's finding is that this particular failure is silent and permanent.
decisions.consequence:
The client sends `X-Logbook-Format: 2` on every read. The server answers `406 {"code":"unsupported_format"}` for anything it cannot emit — a TWELFTH code in DEC-12's vocabulary — and a header naming what it CAN emit. An old client turns that into 'update the app' instead of a silent loop. A missing header is treated as the current version, so the header is additive and an old client that never learned to send it is no worse off than today.
PAIRED WITH A CLIENT-SIDE CIRCUIT BREAKER, in CLIENT-PREREQUISITES: N consecutive decode failures stops the re-fetch. Belt and braces, deliberately, because the failure mode is a phone that cannot be recovered without a reinstall.
